specimens.tldr: Octopuses have three hearts and blue, copper-based blood, so their circulation looks nothing like ours.
Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons live in its arms, so each arm can taste and decide on its own.
Tardigrades can survive the vacuum of space, extreme radiation, and near-total dehydration, then revive.
Sharks are older than trees, having swum the oceans for more than 400 million years.
The jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can revert to an earlier life stage, effectively cheating aging.
Axolotls can regrow entire limbs, parts of their heart, and even portions of their brain.
Honeybees tell each other the direction and distance to food by dancing a looping 'waggle.'
Trees trade nutrients and send warning signals through underground networks of fungal threads.
Bristlecone pines can live more than 4,000 years, older than the pyramids.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, the only known animal to do so.
A hummingbird's heart can beat over 1,000 times a minute while it hovers.
Cephalopods can taste with their skin, sampling chemicals wherever they touch.
Your body is built from roughly 37 trillion cells, each running its own tiny chemistry.
Gut microbes outnumber your own cells and together weigh on the order of a kilogram or two.
Your brain burns about a fifth of your energy despite being only about 2% of your weight.
Nerve signals can race along at over 100 meters per second, faster than a sprinting cheetah.
You shed and regrow most of your skin's outer layer roughly every month.
Memories aren't kept in one spot; they're spread across networks of connected neurons.
A bolt of lightning is roughly five times hotter than the visible surface of the Sun.
Almost all of an atom is empty space; if the nucleus were a marble, electrons would orbit a stadium away.
At its triple point, water can boil and freeze at the same time, coexisting as solid, liquid, and gas.
Nothing with mass can reach light speed, because its energy would have to become infinite.
Sound travels about four times faster through water than through air.
Chilled below about 2 kelvin, liquid helium becomes a frictionless superfluid that climbs its own container walls.
An object's color is simply the light it fails to absorb and bounces back to your eye.
A prism splits white light because each color bends by a slightly different amount as it passes through.
Entangled particles stay linked, so measuring one instantly tells you about the other, however far apart.
Bananas are faintly radioactive thanks to the potassium-40 they contain.
Under the right conditions hot water can freeze faster than cold, the still-debated Mpemba effect.
A day on Venus lasts longer than its entire year, because it spins so slowly.
A teaspoon of neutron-star material would weigh about as much as a mountain on Earth.
There are more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.
Saturn is so low in density that, given a big enough ocean, it would float.
Helium was spotted in the Sun's light before anyone found it on Earth, which is how it got its name.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to cross the 150 million kilometers to Earth.
Olympus Mons on Mars stands nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.
The universe is expanding, and the farther a galaxy is, the faster it rushes away from us.
A single year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years.
The bootprints Apollo astronauts left on the Moon could survive for millions of years.
Honey never truly spoils; sealed pots from ancient tombs are still edible thousands of years later.
Graphene is a sheet of carbon just one atom thick, yet stronger than steel for its weight.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon; only the arrangement of atoms makes one hard and one soft.
Water is unusual in expanding as it freezes, which is why ice floats instead of sinking.
Most of the weight you lose from food actually leaves your body as exhaled carbon dioxide.
Gallium is a metal that melts in your hand, turning liquid just below 30°C.
The Eiffel Tower can stand about 15 cm taller in summer as its iron expands in the heat.
Mount Everest inches a few millimeters higher each year as tectonic plates keep colliding.
The Sahara was green and dotted with lakes just several thousand years ago.
Earth's solid inner core is nearly as hot as the surface of the Sun.
The Pacific Ocean is slowly shrinking while the Atlantic widens, at about the speed your nails grow.
Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth roughly 8 million times every day.
There are more possible games of chess than there are atoms in the observable universe.
As far as anyone has ever computed, the digits of pi never repeat and never end.
In any group of 23 people, it's more likely than not that two share a birthday.
The number zero was a surprisingly late arrival in the history of mathematics.
Some bacteria grow protein 'nanowires' and conduct electricity, effectively breathing through metal.
Extremophile microbes thrive in boiling vents, acid pools, and deep ice where almost nothing else can.
A stretched-out strand of your DNA would run about two meters long, yet coils inside a microscopic nucleus.
Your immune system keeps a memory of past infections, which is exactly why vaccines work.
Old window glass is thicker at the bottom because of how it was made, not because glass slowly flows.
